meta.thesis: CrewAI and Role-based Agents becomes practical when you can map it to a decision, a workflow, and a validation check.

mentalMap.title: CrewAI and Role-based Agents: mental map
mentalMap.caption: Follow the build path: define roles, give them tasks, wire a crew, then harden it.
mentalMap.oneLineThesis: CrewAI lets you build a multi-agent system by defining specialist agents (role + goal + backstory), assigning tasks, and running them as a crew under a process.

modules.title: Why role-based agents exist
modules.sub: Starts the spine: the problem a crew of specialists solves.
modules.summary: One generalist agent given a big, fuzzy goal tends to wander. CrewAI's answer is to split the work across agents that each have a narrow role, goal, and backstory. This module frames why that split is worth the extra moving parts before we open up the pieces.
objectives: Explain the problem role-based agents solve that a single prompt does not.
Name what an agent's role, goal, and backstory each control.
Choose one validation check that would catch a role-confusion failure.

blocks.title: Why one agent isn't enough

spans.text: Before reading on, predict:
if you asked a single agent to "research a topic, then write a polished article about it," what tends to go wrong as the task gets bigger?
Hand one agent a broad goal — research, then write, then fact-check — and it blurs the jobs together: it stops researching too early, edits while it drafts, and loses track of which step it is on.
CrewAI
exists to fix this by splitting the work across several agents, each with a narrow identity.
It is a multi-agent
framework
: a library that defines agents by a role, gives each a task, and runs them together as a crew. The reusable idea is
role-based design
— a focused agent makes better decisions than a generalist with the same model.
Each agent is configured with three fields that do real work:

items.text: role
— the job title ("Senior Researcher"); it scopes what the agent should and should not do.
goal
— the outcome the agent is optimizing for, in one sentence.
backstory
— context that biases tone and judgement ("You value primary sources over blogs").

blocks.title: How sharp is the agent's role?
blocks.caption: Slide from a vague generalist to a sharply scoped specialist and watch the behavior change.

stops.label: No role ("Assistant")
stops.note: Generic identity. The agent does a bit of everything, mixes research with writing, and stops when it feels done.

stops.label: Role + goal
stops.note: "Researcher" with the goal "gather verifiable facts." Behavior tightens — it now knows it is researching, not drafting.

stops.label: Role + goal + backstory
stops.note: Adds "You distrust unsourced claims." The agent now prefers primary sources and flags weak evidence — judgement, not just scope.

blocks.title: How to design a role from a goal

spans.text: Write the role as a job title an org would actually post — "Travel Researcher," not "Helpful AI." If you can't fit it in a title, the scope is too broad and should be split into two agents.

steps.label: State the goal as an outcome

spans.text: The goal is what this agent is optimizing for, not the steps. "Find the three cheapest flights with their constraints" — measurable, and clearly different from the writer's goal.

steps.label: Add a backstory that biases judgement

spans.text: Backstory is where you encode taste and guardrails: "You always confirm price against a primary source before reporting it." This shapes how the agent decides, not just what it is allowed to touch.

blocks.title: Concrete use case: a research-and-write crew

spans.text: Say you want a short market brief on electric scooters. Instead of one agent, you define two:

items.text: Researcher
— role "Market Researcher," goal "collect verifiable facts and figures," backstory "you cite sources and never guess numbers."
Writer
— role "Tech Editor," goal "turn research into a tight 200-word brief," backstory "you write plainly and never add facts the researcher didn't provide."

spans.text: Neither agent does the other's job. The Writer cannot invent statistics because its backstory forbids it, and the Researcher won't ramble because its goal is facts, not prose. That separation is the whole point of role-based design.

blocks.title: Technical note: roles are prompt scaffolding, not enforcement

spans.text: Under the hood, role, goal, and backstory are assembled into the system prompt CrewAI sends to the model. They strongly steer behavior, but they do not hard-enforce it — a Writer agent can still hallucinate a number if the model slips.
Treat the role as guidance, and put real constraints (allowed tools, output schema, a validation step) where they can be checked — not only in the backstory text.

blocks.prompt: What is the main reason CrewAI splits work across role-defined agents instead of using one agent?

options.text: Multiple agents are always cheaper to run than one.
A narrowly scoped agent stays focused and makes better decisions than a generalist on the same model.
CrewAI requires at least two agents to function.

blocks.explanation: Role-based design works because a focused identity (role + goal + backstory) keeps each agent from blurring jobs together. It is about decision quality, not a hard requirement or a cost saving — more agents usually cost more.

modules.title: Agent, Task, and Crew: the three pieces
modules.sub: Names the three objects from module 1's split and how they connect.
modules.summary: Module 1 said CrewAI splits work across roles. This module names the three objects that make that real — Agent, Task, and Crew — and traces how a request flows through them from input to output.
objectives: Name what an Agent, a Task, and a Crew each own.
Trace how a task's output becomes the next agent's context.
Explain why tasks, not agents, carry the actual work description.

blocks.title: Three objects: Agent, Task, Crew

spans.text: A CrewAI program is built from three objects. Keeping their jobs separate is what makes a crew debuggable.

items.text: Agent
— a worker defined by role, goal, and backstory (from module 1), plus the tools it may use. It describes
who
can do work.
Task
— a unit of work: a description, an expected output, and the agent assigned to it. It describes
what
must be done.
Crew
— the container that holds the agents and tasks and runs them under a
process
. It describes
how and in what order
they run.

spans.text: A common surprise: the work description lives on the
Task
, not the Agent. An agent is a reusable specialist; a task is the specific assignment you hand it. The same Researcher agent can run many different research tasks.

blocks.title: How a request flows through a crew

spans.text: You call crew.kickoff(inputs={...}). The crew interpolates those inputs into each task's description (for example a {topic} placeholder).

steps.label: Each task runs on its agent

spans.text: The crew gives task 1 to its assigned agent. The agent runs its own internal loop — reasoning and optionally calling tools — until it produces the task's expected output.

steps.label: Output becomes the next task's context

spans.text: In a sequential crew, task 1's output is passed into task 2 as context. So the Writer sees the Researcher's findings without you wiring anything by hand.

blocks.title: Concrete use case: tracing the brief through the crew

spans.text: Reusing the research-and-write crew from module 1, here is what each object holds at run time:

items.text: Agents
: Researcher and Writer — defined once, no task text inside them.
Task A
: "Research {topic}; output 5 sourced facts." Assigned to Researcher.
Task B
: "Write a 200-word brief." Assigned to Writer; receives Task A's output as context.
Crew
: holds [Researcher, Writer] and [Task A, Task B], runs them sequentially.

spans.text: Calling kickoff(inputs={"topic": "electric scooters"}) fills the {topic} slot, runs Task A, then hands its sourced facts to Task B. The final answer is Task B's output.

blocks.title: Defining the three objects in code
blocks.code:
from crewai import Agent, Task, Crew, Process

researcher = Agent(
    role="Market Researcher",
    goal="Collect 5 verifiable facts about {topic}",
    backstory="You cite sources and never guess numbers.",
)
writer = Agent(
    role="Tech Editor",
    goal="Turn research into a tight 200-word brief",
    backstory="You write plainly and add no facts the researcher didn't provide.",
)

research = Task(
    description="Research {topic}. Output 5 sourced facts.",
    expected_output="A bulleted list of 5 facts, each with a source.",
    agent=researcher,
)
write = Task(
    description="Write a 200-word brief from the research.",
    expected_output="A single 200-word paragraph.",
    agent=writer,
)

crew = Crew(
    agents=[researcher, writer],
    tasks=[research, write],
    process=Process.sequential,
)
result = crew.kickoff(inputs={"topic": "electric scooters"})

spans.text: Notice the work lives on the Task (description + expected_output), the identity lives on the Agent, and order lives on the Crew. The {topic} placeholder is filled by the kickoff inputs.

predictThenReveal.prompt: In a sequential crew, where does the writer get the researcher's facts from? Predict before reading.
predictThenReveal.answer: CrewAI automatically passes the previous task's output as context to the next task — so the write task sees the research task's output without you wiring it explicitly. (You can also pass context=[research] to be explicit.)

syntax.explains: Defines a unit of work and who does it.
Runs tasks in list order, piping each output to the next.
Fills placeholders and runs the crew.

blocks.prompt: In CrewAI, which object carries the description of the actual work to be done?

options.text: The Agent — it holds the work instructions.
The Task — the agent is a reusable specialist; the task is the specific assignment.
The Crew — it stores all instructions centrally.

blocks.explanation: The Task holds the description and expected_output. The Agent supplies identity and tools and can be reused across many tasks; the Crew only sets composition and order.

modules.title: Sequential vs hierarchical process
modules.sub: With the pieces in hand, choose how the crew runs them.
modules.summary: You now have agents and tasks. The crew's process decides how they execute. CrewAI offers two: sequential (a fixed pipeline) and hierarchical (a manager agent delegates). This module is the decision — pick the right one and name what each costs.
objectives: Contrast the sequential and hierarchical crew processes.
Choose a process given control, cost, and flexibility needs.
Explain why hierarchical adds an extra LLM call per delegation.

spans.text: Before reading on, recall from module 1:
what three fields define an agent's identity, and why does a sharper role lead to better decisions?

(The answer: role, goal, and backstory. A sharper role narrows scope and biases judgement, so the agent stops blurring jobs together.) Hold that in mind — the process you pick next decides how much of that focus the framework will protect.

blocks.title: Two ways a crew can run

spans.text: The crew's
process
sets how tasks execute. CrewAI gives you two built-in options.

items.text: Sequential
— tasks run in list order; each output feeds the next. You control the flow exactly. Predictable, cheap, easy to debug.
Hierarchical
— a manager agent (you supply a manager_llm) decides which agent gets which task, delegates, and reviews results. Flexible, but it adds extra LLM calls and unpredictability.

spans.text: Rule of thumb: if you already know the order of steps, sequential is almost always the right starting point. Reach for hierarchical only when the order genuinely depends on intermediate results.

blocks.title: How to choose the process

spans.text: If you can write the steps as a numbered list before running anything (research, then write, then edit), the order is fixed — use sequential.
If the next agent depends on what an earlier one found ("if the data is incomplete, send it back to research"), a manager needs to decide at run time — that's hierarchical.

steps.label: Can you afford the manager's overhead?

spans.text: Each delegation in a hierarchical crew is an extra LLM call by the manager. Budget for more tokens and slower runs before choosing it.

blocks.title: Sequential vs hierarchical

options.name: Sequential process

cells.text: You set the exact order in the task list.
One LLM run per task; no manager overhead.
Pipelines where steps are known up front.

options.whenToUse: Use when the step order is fixed and known before running.

options.name: Hierarchical process

cells.text: A manager agent decides routing at run time.
Extra manager LLM calls per delegation.
Branching work where routing depends on results.

options.whenToUse: Use when the next step genuinely depends on intermediate results.

blocks.howToRead: Default to sequential. Move to hierarchical only when a manager has to make routing decisions you can't write down in advance.

blocks.title: Technical note: the manager is itself an agent

spans.text: In a hierarchical crew you pass a manager_llm. CrewAI spins up an internal manager agent that reads each task, picks a worker, delegates, and judges the result. Every one of those steps is a model call you don't see in the task list.
If your token bill or latency jumps unexpectedly after switching to hierarchical, the manager's hidden delegation calls are usually the cause.

blocks.prompt: When should you reach for a hierarchical crew instead of a sequential one?

options.text: Whenever you have more than two agents.
When the routing between agents depends on intermediate results and can't be fixed in advance.
Whenever you want the crew to run faster and cheaper.

blocks.explanation: Hierarchical exists for run-time routing decisions a manager must make. It is slower and more expensive (extra manager calls), so it is not the choice for speed or for a simple count of agents.

modules.decisionItForces: Choose the crew process for CrewAI and Role-based Agents: a fixed sequential pipeline or a manager-led hierarchical crew.

modules.title: Build a minimal crew
modules.sub: Turn the pieces and the process choice into running code.
modules.summary: Modules 2 and 3 gave you the objects and the process. Here you assemble the smallest crew that actually runs, finish a completion problem where the key line is left as a TODO, and learn how to check AI-generated crew code before trusting it.
objectives: Assemble a two-agent sequential crew that runs end to end.
Complete a crew where one wiring line is missing.
Verify AI-generated CrewAI code against a short checklist.

blocks.title: The smallest crew that runs

spans.text: A minimal working crew needs only four things: at least one Agent, at least one Task assigned to an agent, a Crew that lists both, and a kickoff call. Module 2's code was exactly this shape — here you make it run and then extend it.
The pattern to internalize: define specialists once, describe work as tasks, wire them with a
process
, and let CrewAI pipe each task's output forward. Everything bigger is a variation on this skeleton.

blocks.title: Assembling the crew, step by step

spans.text: Create each Agent with role, goal, and backstory. No task text here — keep them reusable.
Each Task gets a description, an expected_output, and an agent=. The expected_output is what tells the agent when it is done.

steps.label: Build and kick off the crew

spans.text: Pass the agents and tasks to Crew(...), set process=Process.sequential, and call kickoff(inputs=...). The return value is the last task's output.

blocks.title: Concrete use case: what running it looks like

spans.text: When you call kickoff on the research-and-write crew, the run unfolds like this:

items.text: The Researcher runs its task, possibly calling a search tool, and returns 5 sourced facts.
CrewAI passes those facts as context into the Writer's task.
The Writer produces the 200-word brief, which is returned as the crew's result.

spans.text: You wrote no glue code between the two steps — the sequential process handled the handoff.

blocks.title: Completion problem: finish the crew
blocks.code:
from crewai import Agent, Task, Crew, Process

planner = Agent(
    role="Trip Planner",
    goal="Draft a 3-day {city} itinerary",
    backstory="You build realistic, walkable day plans.",
)
budgeter = Agent(
    role="Budget Reviewer",
    goal="Add a cost estimate to each day",
    backstory="You flag any day over $150.",
)

plan = Task(
    description="Plan 3 days in {city}.",
    expected_output="A day-by-day itinerary.",
    agent=planner,
)
review = Task(
    description="Add per-day cost estimates and flags.",
    expected_output="The itinerary with costs.",
    agent=budgeter,
)

crew = Crew(
    agents=[planner, budgeter],
    tasks=[plan, review],
    process=Process.sequential,
)
# TODO: run the crew for city="Lisbon" and capture the result
result = ___

spans.text: Everything is wired except the final line. Decide what call fills the TODO so the crew actually runs with the city supplied, then reveal the answer.

predictThenReveal.prompt: What should replace the ___ on the last line so the crew runs for Lisbon?
predictThenReveal.answer: result = crew.kickoff(inputs={"city": "Lisbon"})  — kickoff fills the {city} placeholder in both task descriptions and runs the tasks in order, returning the final (review) task's output.

syntax.explains: Tells each agent what 'done' looks like.
Runs plan, then review, piping output forward.

spans.text: If an AI assistant writes a CrewAI script for you, check these before running it:

items.text: Every Task has an agent= assigned
— an unassigned task silently has no one to run it.
Each Task has a concrete expected_output
— without it agents tend to over-run or stop early.
The process matches the task order
— sequential assumes the list is in execution order; check that it is.
Placeholders match the kickoff inputs
— a {topic} in a description with no "topic" key passed in will not interpolate.

blocks.prompt: What is the minimum a CrewAI program needs to run?

options.text: A manager LLM and at least three agents.
At least one agent, at least one task assigned to it, a crew listing them, and a kickoff call.
A LangGraph state object and a compiled graph.

blocks.explanation: A minimal crew is one Agent, one Task assigned to it, a Crew holding both, and crew.kickoff(). A manager LLM is only for the hierarchical process, and CrewAI does not use LangGraph graphs.

modules.title: Where crews break, and how to harden them
modules.sub: Closes the spine: the failure modes a running crew still hits.
modules.summary: A crew that works in a demo can still loop, drift off-role, or burn tokens in production. This module names the realistic failure modes of multi-agent crews and the checks that contain them, then forces the decision: ship the simple crew, or invest in hardening.
objectives: Recognize the common ways a multi-agent crew fails in practice.
Map each failure mode to a concrete guardrail.
Decide when a crew is ready to ship versus needing more rigor.

spans.text: Before reading on, recall from module 3:
why does the hierarchical process cost more than sequential?
(The answer: the manager agent makes extra LLM calls to decide routing and review results.) Keep that in mind — runaway manager calls are one of the failure modes below.

blocks.title: How crews break in practice

spans.text: Knowing the happy path isn't enough. These are the failure modes that show up once a crew leaves the demo.

items.text: Role drift / job blur.
An agent with a fuzzy role starts doing a neighboring agent's job — the Writer invents facts, the Researcher starts editing. The fix is sharper roles and an output schema, not a longer backstory.
Delegation loops.
In a hierarchical crew the manager keeps re-delegating because no task ever satisfies it. Set a max_iter and clear expected_output so 'done' is recognizable.
Runaway token cost.
Long backstories, full task outputs passed forward, and manager calls compound. Watch the bill and trim context that the next agent doesn't need.
Silent context loss.
A late task assumes information an earlier task never actually put in its output. Pin dependencies explicitly with context=[...] rather than trusting order alone.

blocks.title: Turning a failure mode into a guardrail

spans.text: Read the trace. Repeated tool calls, the manager re-delegating, or an agent producing the wrong kind of output each point to a specific failure mode above.
Add the matching guardrail: tighter expected_output for job blur, max_iter for loops, explicit context for silent loss, a token budget for cost.
Run the same input again and confirm the symptom is gone in the trace before declaring it fixed — not just that the final answer looks right.

options.name: Simple baseline

cells.text: Fast way to learn or prove value.

options.whenToUse: Use first when the outcome is still uncertain.

options.name: Production design

cells.text: Best when users depend on the result.

options.whenToUse: Use when quality, safety, or uptime matters.

options.name: Advanced optimization
options.whenToUse: Use only after traces show the baseline is insufficient.

blocks.howToRead: Pick the smallest option that satisfies the user-visible requirement and can be tested.

blocks.title: Technical note

spans.text: The technical habit is to make hidden state visible: record inputs, outputs, parameters, and the source or version that shaped the result.
If a claim would matter in a production review, attach a source or a test to it.

blocks.prompt: Which statement best captures the point of "Production checklist" in CrewAI and Role-based Agents?

options.text: It is a named concept to memorize.
It is a design boundary with inputs, outputs, tradeoffs, and tests.
It should always be solved with the largest available model.

blocks.explanation: The reusable skill is mapping a concept or tool to the decision it changes and the test that proves it works.
